expectations.text: Output mentions Manski reflection problem or the linear-in-means identification failure
expectations.evidence: Dedicated section 'Problem 1: The Manski reflection problem' — 'Manski (1993) showed that in the linear-in-means model, the endogenous peer effect... and the correlated effect... are not separately identified from cross-sectional observational data... OLS on peer means conflates influence with selection.'

expectations.text: Output mentions Shalizi-Thomas confounding or the homophily-contagion confound
expectations.evidence: Dedicated section 'Problem 2: The Shalizi-Thomas confound' — 'Shalizi & Thomas (2011) generalize this into the network setting with a stronger result: homophily and contagion are generically confounded in observational network data.'

expectations.text: Output does NOT claim the regression identifies causal peer effects
expectations.evidence: 'But it does not identify a causal peer influence effect' and 'The β = 0.43 therefore reflects a blend of influence, selection, and shared environment in unknown proportions' and 'It is not evidence of peer influence on smoking as stated.'

expectations.text: Output correctly specifies that SAOM/RSiena requires longitudinal panel data with at least 2 waves AND observable network change between waves — NOT just cross-sectional data
expectations.evidence: 'SAOM requires panel data — at minimum 2 waves with observable changes between waves, and ideally 3+ waves. The network must show real change between waves (if the friendship structure is essentially frozen, selection is not observed), and behavior must also change... SAOM cannot be run on your current cross-sectional data.'

expectations.text: Output mentions Bramoullé et al. IV/GMM or friends-of-friends instruments as a cross-sectional identification strategy (not just 'use SAOM')
expectations.evidence: 'Bramoullé, Djebbari & Fortin (2009) show that the reflection problem can be overcome in a network setting... if your network contains intransitive triads... friends-of-friends' characteristics affect i's outcome only through their effect on j's behavior, so they serve as instruments (IVs) for peers' outcomes... This is the Bramoullé et al. GMM/IV approach.'
